articles.title: Israel would rather not watch NAZA
articles.summary: The backlash against the Gaza documentary is part of a broader refusal to confront the reality of the genocide.
articles.body:
NAZA (Hebrew acronym for “collateral damage”), the documentary made by Yuval Avraham and Rachel Szor, has yet to secure an Israeli distributor or a public screening, despite its creators’ stated intention to show it widely in the country. Various senior executives, from the Israeli military chief of staff to the minister of culture, promised that they were about to “take steps” against the creators of the film. Other than stripping them of their Israeli citizenship (considered a remarkably rare measure), what those “steps” could be was unclear. However, one refrain dominated the outrage directed at Avraham and Szor: Those condemning the film had no intention of watching it.

It is important to emphasise that this oath to refrain from watching the film was authentic. In a way, it is a variation on a theme that became prevalent throughout the first months of the “war”. When images of devastation began to emerge from Gaza, many Israelis wrote that they could feel no pity for the children of Gaza (at the end of 2023, the number of children killed and orphaned was already known and difficult to grasp, as were military “procedures”). These Israelis said they had “closed their hearts” in response to the huge, intentional death toll in the Israeli towns and villages surrounding Gaza. They claimed they would not and could not feel pity for anyone who had committed such atrocities, or for anyone related to them. Activists on the Israeli left believed that if Israelis were exposed to images from the already nearly deleted Gaza, they would head for the streets and call for a stop to the war. These activists were soundly rebuffed.

NAZA was, itself, a rebuttal of the position actively taken by the Israeli media – “Yes, the Israeli military had made mistakes but these should be investigated by the military and the Israeli legal system, both very much capable of carrying out the task.” Raviv Drucker, perhaps Israel’s most prominent investigative journalist, when asked by Yuval Avraham (during an interview of Avraham himself conducted by Drucker) why Israeli media had done nothing to expose the methods of killing documented by NAZA, said with visible embarrassment that doing so was “difficult” for a host of reasons. However, Drucker was also quick to add that if it were up to him, he would not have aired the film because he believed it lacked journalistic professionalism, relying as it does on anonymous testimony. This line of criticism was quickly taken up by other journalists considered a part of the Israeli left. They attacked the film and its creators, accusing them of everything from seeking money and attention to actively working for Israel’s downfall in the service of Netanyahu and Qatar. They were called “useful idiots”, meaning people who work for a worthy cause but are unwittingly used in the service of another. Journalists like Uri Misgav acknowledged the importance of criticism but implied that NAZA served the goals of Israel’s enemies. They suggested that its disregard for journalistic standards showed that the creators had already reached their conclusion: That Israel was the root of all evil and solely responsible for the state of Gaza.

For Israelis, not watching NAZA is a point of pride. Some will cite the lack of journalistic standards (this from a country that assassinated more than 200 journalists over the course of its genocide in Gaza). Other Israelis will suggest that they recognise “treason” when they see it. Many Israelis will apply the following wondrous excuse: “Even if some of this is true, you wash your dirty laundry at home; you don’t entertain others by using that dirty laundry to demonstrate that Israel really is responsible for the killing of 20,000 children and more than 70,000 Palestinians in Gaza.” The fact that the military and the Israeli legal system have proven themselves to be incompetent at best (and thoroughly politicised at worst) when investigating war crimes and crimes against humanity is beside the point for many Israelis. After all, one could offer up such incompetence as an excuse for the strategies exposed by NAZA. Israelis wouldn’t hear of it. This is yet another example of the world’s hatred for Israel (“anti-Semitism”, if you like) that makes international accusations levelled against Israel completely irrelevant. No matter what we do, we will emerge at fault, so why encourage this state of affairs by having lengthy discussions about a critical movie? We’ve heard the criticism countless times. We know there is a web of detractors all over the world (perhaps funded by Qatar, perhaps by the Red-Green alliance between the woke left and radical Islam). It doesn’t matter.

Just as Israelis “closed their hearts” when the genocide began, so they are shutting their eyes and ears now. They take pride in their ignorance of the film’s content. They feel it misrepresents them. How do they know? They don’t, but that only makes them even more convinced of the one-sidedness of the whole episode. It is enough to hear that the directors received an unprecedented 25-minute standing ovation at the Venice Film Festival, where they won a special jury prize. Special, eh? Everything about Israel is special. A special prize can simply be invented on the spot to present Israel negatively. It isn’t as though Avraham and Szor walked away from the podium with the Silver Lion, one of the festival’s major awards, is it? Their film is not art. Nor is it a documentary because it doesn’t observe the codes of documentary filmmaking. Its only purpose is to discredit Israel, isn’t it? If that is the case, why should an Israeli with any sense of identity do the enemy’s work: The ultimate destruction of Israel as a Jewish state (democracy was abandoned right at the start), for them? Better to deny and reject reality. It isn’t just that we do what we want – we are the ones who define the very nature of reality itself. When we don’t like it, we close our eyes and wait for the threat to pass. It always does.

articles.title: Tukaram Mundhe says Shah Rukh Khan, Ajay Devgn, Tiger Shroff are violators of the law as he speaks on their elaichi ad row: 'There is a responsibility cast upon the person who is advertising it'
articles.summary: Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration (FDA) commissioner Tukaram Mundhe has made it clear that celebrity status will not prevent Shah Rukh Khan, Aj.
articles.body: Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration (FDA) commissioner Tukaram Mundhe has made it clear that celebrity status will not prevent Shah Rukh Khan, Ajay Devgn and Tiger Shroff from facing action over their association with a Vimal Elaichi advertisement. The three actors were issued show-cause notices by the Maharashtra FDA over allegations that the campaign amounted to surrogate advertising for Vimal Pan Masala, a product prohibited in the state.Mundhe said the FDA has already initiated adjudication and prosecution proceedings against one of the actors who did not respond to the notice within the stipulated time.“According to you they may be stars, but according to me they are only advertisers in this case. So I am looking at them as violators of the law, and the law will take its own course. That’s why we have started taking action,” Mundhe said in an interview with NDTV.The notices were issued on August 11, giving the three actors 15 days to submit their responses. According to Mundhe, two actors replied to the notices, while one did not. He did not disclose their identities.“We have taken this action as per the law,” he said.“In one case where they have not responded, we are starting the adjudicating and prosecution proceedings,” Mundhe added.The two actors who responded reportedly argued that the responsibility should lie with the manufacturer. Mundhe said their submissions will be considered during the hearing before the FDA takes further action.“We are giving them a hearing. My officer, the assistant commissioner who issued the notices, will be giving the hearing,” he said.When asked specifically if Shah Rukh Khan’s team had submitted a response, Mundhe said, “Most likely he has not responded, but I’m not too sure about it.”Mundhe also rejected the argument that celebrities endorsing a product cannot be held responsible because the manufacturer is ultimately behind it. He pointed to advertising provisions under the Food Safety Act, which, according to him, place specific responsibilities on advertisers.“There are clearly advertising regulations as per the Food Safety Act. [The regulations] talk about who the advertiser is, and there is a responsibility very specifically cast upon the person or institution who is advertising. There is a responsibility cast upon the person who is advertising it, including to take due diligence about what he or she is endorsing. To say that it is not upon them is wrong… Not only morally, but legally I’m talking about, because I am here as a regulator,” he said.Shah Rukh Khan has previously spoken about his decision to endorse products that are legally available for sale. During an interview with CNN-IBN, journalist Karan Thapar had questioned the actor about celebrities promoting products considered unhealthy. Khan had said, “I would appeal to any authority to ban it; don’t let it be sold in our country. If smoking is bad, stop the production of cigarettes. If you think soft drinks are bad, don’t allow them to be made. My logic is you’re not stopping them because they bring in revenue. You’re not stopping certain products because they’re revenue sources for the government. Then don’t stop my revenue. I’m an actor. I’m supposed to do a job and earn from it. And very clearly, if you think something is wrong, stop it. Stop making it.”Ajay Devgn, who has been associated with Vimal campaigns for several years, had also addressed the criticism surrounding his endorsement in 2022. Defending his association with the brand, the actor had said he was promoting elaichi and not pan masala.“It is a personal choice. When you do something, you also see how harmful it would be. Some things are harmful, some are not. I would say it without naming it because I don’t want to promote it; I was doing elaichi. What I feel is that, more than advertisements, if certain things are so wrong, then they should not be sold,” he had told SCREEN.Akshay Kumar was previously part of the Vimal Elaichi campaign alongside Shah Rukh Khan and Ajay Devgn in 2022. Following the backlash, Kumar apologised and announced that he was stepping away from the brand. He also said that he would donate the money he received as his endorsement fee to a cause. Tiger Shroff subsequently joined the campaign in his place.The legal proceedings also saw a development on September 14, when the Delhi High Court dismissed a petition filed by PB Agro LLP, the master licensee for Vimal Elaichi. The company had approached the court seeking to quash the notices issued to Shah Rukh Khan, Ajay Devgn and Tiger Shroff.Justice Swarana Kanta Sharma held that the Delhi High Court did not have territorial jurisdiction to hear the matter, as the notices had been issued by the Maharashtra FDA in Mumbai.Get the latest Bollywood & Entertainment News, and more. articles.title: Food festivals across UK targeted by AI scam, BBC finds
articles.summary: One trader says her "heart sank" after discovering she had lost money through a scam festival invitation.
articles.body:
British food festivals are being used to target small food and craft businesses in a scam made possible by artificial intelligence (AI).

A BBC Wales investigation found dozens of traders received professional-looking emails purporting to be from festivals with any requests for money only coming after multiple emails are exchanged.

One trader whose "heart sank" when she discovered she had lost money, said that despite spotting scams regularly, the multiple emails she exchanged were "so realistic" that she fell for one.

Abergavenny Food Festival said the accessibility of AI meant scammers could reach more people with scams that look "far more believable".

Harriet Thomas had applied for a stand at the Abergavenny Food Festival on previous years, and was "really excited" when an email came offering her the opportunity to book a place for her knitting workshops.

She said that as she spent so much time on a computer running her business, she was used to seeing scams, but this time "nothing sparked a red flag".

Unlike other scam emails, the one in question "looked completely genuine" including the email address it had been sent from.

"[I] filled in a jot form, which is something we use all the time and again, all the fonts, everything, [and] the branding was completely legitimate," she said.

She said she had been reassured by subsequent email exchanges which used her name and showed the sender had detailed knowledge of the Abergavenny festival site and facilities on offer, until she finally paid for a pitch.

It was only after she published a Facebook post to say she would be at the festival, that she saw a social media post from the real one warning about the scam emails.

"My heart just sank. I was so embarrassed," she said.

Despite publicising her experience to warn other traders and reporting the scam, she said she did not know how they could be stopped.

"It's getting more and more competitive to try and get a stall at these events. So people are more likely to fill a form in quickly thinking, I really, really want to make sure I secure my space," she said.

Scam emails seen by BBC Wales have used the branding, details and even the names of staff from food festivals right across the country, including Narberth, York, Broadmead, Ludlow, Mold, the Forest of Dean, Newport and St Fagans.

Andy Fryers who coordinates Abergavenny Food Festival said the number and credibility of the scams it had seen had made things "much more difficult" for them this year.

There was no conclusive proof the scam was powered by AI, but experts have said it would not have been possible five years ago.

"I think it's the evolution of AI and the easy accessibility of it now," Fryers said.

"Anyone can get on to Claude or ChatGPT, or whichever one you want to go with, and within a few minutes get it to search out all traders in a certain area, get contact details, search our website, get contact details, make up a couple of Gmail accounts.

"It's very straightforward and quite cheap and you can blanket approach these things."

The most recent figures from Report Fraud - the reporting service for cyber crime and fraud across England, Wales and Northern Ireland - echo that, with an increase of 395% in reports which were linked to AI during 2025-26 compared to the previous year.

With many festivals run by volunteers and attended by small, local traders, Fryers said seeing the emails that used his name had initially been a shock.

"You can feel like this person is targeting you, and when we first started getting these it felt a little bit like someone trying to do over the festival," he said.

"But actually you realise when you start seeing other festivals being targeted by the same thing, you realise actually it's not. This is a computer-generated thing.

"Obviously someone's putting it in but... it isn't personal, it's just someone trying to scam you, it's just someone trying to make a quick buck."

Another local company paid £400 to the scammers and bought stock to sell at the festival before they realised they had been scammed.

The festival managed to find space for them at a discounted price, but organisers said they worried that if others turn up on the day having been caught out, it may not be possible to help them also.

Giles Mason, who runs the Take 5 to Stop Fraud campaign at UK Finance which represents the banking and finance industry, said scam emails used to be "riddled with spelling mistakes, poor grammar".

"The use of AI means that that has been wiped out, and also using sort of official looking imagery, graphics, to make it look as convincing as possible as well," he said.

He said that targeting sole traders or volunteer-run operations was an attempt to bypass the security systems of big companies like banks who have had to "invest heavily in stopping scams and building very secure systems to protect their customers".

Two-thirds of these types of scams now start through contact online.

But with £1.3 billion stolen through fraud and scams, last year, he said that if you receive an email, call or text, "particularly if it's out of the blue, just take that moment to stop and think".

He said: "If it's a genuine organisation, they won't mind you taking that moment to stop.

"Go to the company's official website and contact the organisation through the details on there so you know you're dealing with them direct and not with the scammer."

articles.title: Tom Cruise Says Taylor Swift Was ‘Schooling Me on Football’ at Chiefs Game, Calls Her a ‘Brilliant Musician and Director’
articles.summary: Tom Cruise and Taylor Swift made headlines on Monday when they sat next to each other at the Kansas City Chiefs’ first game of the season. But what were the...
articles.body:
Tom Cruise and Taylor Swift made headlines on Monday when they sat next to each other at the Kansas City Chiefs' first game of the season. But what were the two megastars talking about?

"She was schooling me on football. For real," Cruise revealed to Jimmy Fallon during an appearance on "The Tonight Show" on Thursday. But that wasn't the first time Cruise and Swift have had a meeting of the minds — he was spotted at her Eras Tour in London in 2024, and when the pop star married Chiefs tight end Travis Kelce in July, Cruise was in attendance.

"First of all, she's a genius. I've been following her since she was a kid," Cruise said of Swift. "Everybody there, all their friends — they're a beautiful couple and magical in their own right."

And Swift has real ball knowledge. "Oh, she knows her stuff," Cruise continued, adding that the singer "knew nothing about football when she met Travis."

Other than Swift coaching him through the game, Cruise said they "talked about music and movies."

"She's funny, she's got such a great sense of humor," he said. "A brilliant writer also, by the way. A brilliant musician and director — very skilled."

Swift has directed many of her own music videos over the years, and delved further into filmmaking with 2021's "All Too Well: The Short Film," starring Sadie Sink and Dylan O'Brien. In late 2022, it was announced that she would be making her feature directorial debut for Searchlight Pictures, though her record-breaking Eras Tour that began the next year (and extended through December 2024) seems to have delayed this .

Elsewhere in his interview with Fallon, Cruise was asked about rumors that his new film "Digger," directed by Alejandro González Iñárritu, was actually a musical.

"No, but I think it's a very good idea," he laughed. "I think we should do 'Digger' the musical. Digger down!" Cruise and Fallon then broke out into song and dance in their seats.

Cruise's press tour for "Digger" will also include an appearance on Travis and Jason Kelce's "New Heights" podcast, releasing on Friday.

articles.summary: Lo explica en su última aparición en el programa de Jimmy Kimmel
articles.body: Nicole Kidman es una enamorada de España, pero concretamente de una isla. La de Ibiza y cuando puede acude a ella como parte liberadora del día a día. En ella se siente feliz. En la última aparición de la actriz en el programa de Jimmy Kimmel le preguntó si no había ido a la isla española y el conductor del mismo le dijo que no apostillando si se le había perdido algo allí. Pero ella salió con lo enamorada que está del lugar y de su fiesta. La artista se sinceró al señalar que lo que más le apasiona es salir a "bailar". Es más, Kidman reconoció que le encanta acudir a raves, pero, claro, esos eventos multitudinarios donde hay tanta gente que un famoso pueda estar en el lugar puede resultarle estresante por miradas, solicitad de fotos y demás... Ahora bien Kidman tiene una estrategia que ha implementado con el paso del tiempo y que le hace pasar desapercibida. Kidman lo tenia claro. Tiene sus estrategias. Las ha puesto en práctica y le han funcionado. Pasa totalmente inadvertida y goza con lo que más le gusta. "Me pongo gafas. A veces llevo una pequeña peluca oscura para esconderme y entonces puedo simplemente bailar", señalaba. De hecho, la artista se adapta perfectamente al horario español. "Ceno a la hora española, sobre las 22:30 horas, y tras la sobremesa voy al club sobre la una de la madrugada". Y lo goza hasta altas horas e incluso madrugadas... Kidman se siente bien porque hace lo que quiere y hace todo lo posible para que nadie la reconozca con lo que logra su principal objetivo. "Mientras esté rodeada de gente (sus amigos cercanos), estoy bien. Lo necesito", al tiempo que se vanagloriaba de su 'modus operandi': "Soy sigilosa. Soy buena entrando y saliendo de todas partes sin que me vean".

articles.summary: Marathi film ‘Gondhal’, written and directed by Santosh Davakhar, has been selected as India’s official entry for the 99th Academy Awards, the Film Fe.
articles.body: Marathi film ‘Gondhal’, written and directed by Santosh Davakhar, has been selected as India’s official entry for the 99th Academy Awards, the Film Federation of India announced on Friday. The film will represent India in the International Feature Film category at the Oscars 2027.Set against the backdrop of rural Maharashtra, ‘Gondhal’ unfolds over the course of a night during a traditional ritual centred around a newly married couple. The film was chosen from a list of 33 contenders, with P Seshadri serving as the chairperson of the selection committee, according to PTI.The selection marks another milestone for Marathi cinema at the Academy Awards. ‘Gondhal’ becomes the fourth Marathi film to be chosen as India’s official Oscar entry, following ‘Shwaas’ (2005), ‘Harishchandrachi Factory’ (2009) and ‘Court’ (2015).Santosh Davakhar’s film has also previously earned recognition at the International Film Festival of India, where he won the Silver Peacock for Best Director for ‘Gondhal’.Last year, India had selected Neeraj Ghaywan’s ‘Homebound’ as its official submission for the Oscars. However, the film did not secure a nomination.India is yet to win the Best International Feature Film category, which was earlier known as the Best Foreign Language Film category. Three Indian films have received nominations in the category so far — Mehmood Khan’s ‘Mother India’, Mira Nair’s ‘Salaam Bombay’ and Ashutosh Gowariker’s ‘Lagaan’. articles.title: Sydney Sweeney’s provocative sports ad 'reinforces the image she has already built' despite backlash: expert
articles.summary: Sydney Sweeney's nude sports trading app ad drew backlash from Olympic athletes, but PR experts say it may not damage her brand at all.
articles.body: Sydney Sweeney sparked widespread backlash following the release of her provocative campaign for a sports trading app. No stranger to controversy or criticism, Sweeney, 29, faced the music from Olympic athletes, entertainment icons and millions of keyboard warriors who voiced their opinions of the naked ad. Adrienne Uthe, founder of Kronus Communications, exclusively told Fox News Digital that while Sweeney's latest ad may have ruffled feathers, "women having agency also means allowing women to make choices about their image that other women may not personally agree with." SYDNEY SWEENEY FIRES BACK AT TROLLS AFTER FACING CRITICISM ONLINE FOR PROVOCATIVE SPORTS AD "People are entitled to dislike the ad, just like women athletes are entitled to criticize it for their own reasons," Uthe said. "But I don't think this is materially damaging to Sydney Sweeney in any way, shape or form. "In fact, I don't think it's a large departure from who she is and what her brand represents. She's a beautiful woman right now at the peak of her career, and she ultimately can decide which projects she wants to take and which ones she doesn't." She added, "And she's chosen to make sexuality a part of her brand for better or for worse." WATCH HERE: EXPERT WEIGHS IN ON SYDNEY SWEENEY PROVOCATIVE AD CONTROVERSY Sweeney's latest ad featured several shots with strategically placed sports equipment covering her mostly nude body. "Think you know sports? Prove it. Novig is just sports. So, they wanted a show," the "Euphoria" star said in the campaign. SYDNEY SWEENEY, SCOOTER BRAUN ROMANCE FACES BIGGEST CHALLENGE YET AS EXPERT WARNS COUPLE TO 'BE PREPARED' Several female athletes didn’t appear to take too kindly to the ad. Australian Olympic gold medalist swimmer Ariarne Titmus, British sprinter Amy Hunt and former American gymnast Gracie Kramer were among those to denounce the ad. Uthe believed Novig's creative team accomplished its goal, but stressed the significance of effective marketing. "Going viral tells me they captured attention. It doesn’t tell me they captured the customer," Uthe said. "This is where social media completely distorts reality, and we've seen this across all platforms in pop culture, politics, sports and beyond. So the narrative that is the loudest isn't necessarily what is true and what the majority opinion is." PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE Uthe noted that one side claimed the ad objectified women in sports, while the other narrative questions why there's outrage over an obviously provocative ad. "Once one of those frames takes over, whether it's through different content that someone is viewing or someone just inherently has a bias for this topic, that perception is really gonna make it a reality for them," Uthe said. "And that's why I always say, if you can make it trend, you can it true." Olivia Bennett, senior account director at Go Up, thought that the campaign was simply "bad for women in sport." "I can understand the commercial calculation behind choosing Sydney Sweeney," Bennett told Fox News Digital. "Novig will know its audience, and Sydney has built a public brand where sex appeal, provocation and controversy consistently generate attention. "But this was a national campaign. When you choose someone with such a heavily sexualized and frequently controversial public image, you know the campaign is going to travel far beyond your existing customer base. The wider reaction was entirely foreseeable." LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS Bennett believed that the bigger issue at hand was what the ad said about women in sports. "What I find most telling is that female athletes themselves are now pushing back and saying: this isn’t how we want women in sport to be represented," she said. "Once the people who actually work and compete in that world start using your campaign as an example of the problem, you have a much bigger reputational issue than a few negative comments online." She added, "For Sydney, I don’t think the campaign is off-brand at all. If anything, it reinforces the image she has already built. But that doesn’t make it good for women in sport. Personal-brand fit doesn’t remove the wider impact of the message you’re putting into the world." "It's gamedayyyy," the blonde bombshell wrote before tagging the newly launched sports platform. While many comments encouraged "The Housemaid" actress, Sweeney was hit with accusations of sexualizing a predominantly male-dominated field. "As a former athlete and a woman who has personally experienced sexualized comments, I’m genuinely disgusted and deeply disappointed by this campaign," one user wrote. "We’ve spent years fighting to be seen and respected for our talent, strength, and achievements-not reduced to our bodies." "The campaign was about embracing a fun idea," Sweeney said in a statement, according to Variety. "The concept is simple: cut through the noise and put the focus entirely on sports. articles.title: New movies to watch this weekend: See Zach Cregger's 'Resident Evil' in theaters, rent 'The End of Oak Street,' stream 'The Best of the Best' on Netflix
articles.summary: "Resident Evil" gets a thrilling new adaptation, Ethan Hawke teams up with Russell Crowe and a new "Shaun the Sheep" sequel gives families a treat.
articles.body:
Welcome to Trust Me, I Watch Everything , a weekly guide to notable new movies opening or becoming available each Friday.

This week's buzziest release is Zach Cregger's reboot of the Resident Evil franchise, which takes things in an extremely different direction from the previous seven movies. Ethan Hawke's low-budget thriller The Weight is also worth seeking out.

If you'd rather stay home, you can now rent or buy The End of Oak Street, the dinosaurs-in-the-suburbs sci-fi flick starring Anne Hathaway and Ewan McGregor, or catch a hangout vibe with Tony , the Anthony Bourdain biopic of sorts starring Dominic Sessa. Matthew McConaughey's transcendent The Rivals of Amziah King is another one worth the rental fee.

Want to stick to a streaming service you're likely already paying for? Netflix's Best of the Best is a charming coming-of-age comedy, and Shudder has a new original horror flick, Goody Goody.

Why you should see it in a theater: There have already been seven Resident Evil movies — six of them in a more action-oriented series starring Milla Jovovich, four of which were directed by her husband, Paul W.S. Anderson, plus an unrelated "reboot" in 2021 called Welcome to Raccoon City that went for more of a John Carpenter vibe and was more of an attempt to truly "adapt" the games. There's also a Netflix TV show version that ran for a single season in 2022. Countless other works in the horror genre have unofficially cribbed from the Resident Evil games over the years. It's an incredibly influential series.

And yet, Zach Cregger, hot off his Oscar-winning original horror film Weapons, is the first filmmaker to truly feel like he's adapting the experience of playing the games, arguably the scariest survival-horror ones ever made, rather than simply incorporating story and plot elements to explain the outbreak of infected people. In Cregger's hands, Resident Evil is pure crowd-pleasing popcorn cinema, best experienced in a packed movie theater with dozens of other people reacting loudly to the madness.

The premise couldn't be simpler — and the runtime a brisk 90 minutes — as we follow a medical courier named Bryan (Austin Abrams, proving himself to be the Bruce Campbell for a new generation) who unwittingly finds himself fighting for survival as one fateful, horrifying night collapses around him in a swirl of chaos. Fans of the video games will recognize various Easter eggs and nods to game mechanics, including the importance of conserving ammo and checking every last drawer for more of it.

But you don't need to be familiar with the games at all to enjoy the movie, which is an efficient horror set-piece machine that just keeps putting Abrams in increasingly concerning situations. I can't stress enough how much this is a one-man show anchored by Abrams, and he crushes it. He's in every scene, earning tons of laughs simply by reacting as a normal person would in this situation; he's a true audience-surrogate character, ushering us through the chaos. His comedic timing, paired with Cregger's assured camerawork and editing, is a match made in genre-movie heaven.

I didn't expect it to be so heavily inspired by genre classics like The Thing and Evil Dead. In fact, it's a better Evil Dead movie than the last several movies with " Evil Dead " in the title, nailing the horror-comedy tone that only Sam Raimi and a few others can pull off with aplomb. Cregger has a ton of fun with the various monstrous forms that the infected take here, from fusing multiple humans together to crafting his own horror take on a big, scary guy like Dune 's Baron Harkonnen. Resident Evil movies have thus far treated the zombies as pretty traditional movie zombies; Cregger's version gets at the attempt to create the next stage of human evolution.

Zach Cregger's Resident Evil may not feature characters that gaming fans recognize, but it's spiritually more in line with the games than any of the ones that do. Adaptation stuff aside, it's also just a heart-pounding, adrenaline-fueled roller-coaster ride of a movie that has no grander ambitions than getting a rise out of the audience over and over again. It's a blast, and this time, you can't pause it, put your controller down and walk away when things get too intense.

What other critics are saying: The previous seven installments were panned by critics every time; the opposite is true here, as Cregger's take sports a near-perfect score on Rotten Tomatoes. The Independent's Clarisse Loughrey writes, "It feels thoroughly like a film by Zach Cregger ... proving that subtle, psychological work isn't always the superior horror when you have a filmmaker who can deliver a jump scare shock with this much elegant panache." Jesse Hassenger at the Guardian writes, " Resident Evil has a streamlined single-mindedness, and as it barrels through its gamified plot, the tension and entertainment value never flag."

How to watch: Resident Evil is now playing in theaters nationwide.

Why I liked it: The 1953 movie The Wages of Fear, based on the 1950 novel by Georges Arnaud , was famously remade by William Friedkin in 1977 as Sorcerer , which, just as famously, bombed miserably at the box office due to its opening on the heels of a little-known sci-fi flick called Star Wars.

Sorcerer is an incredible movie that has, thankfully, become a cult classic. After decades of being hard to find, it's recently been restored in 4K and regularly plays at repertory cinemas. Friedkin considered it to be his finest work.

All of which is to say that The Weight is a Depression-era survival thriller heist Western that feels heavily inspired by Sorcerer, but made on a minuscule budget and under far less strenuous circumstances. It's tense, well-acted and a worthy take on the doomed men-on-a-mission movie. Imagine if Sorcerer took place during the Oregon Trail days.

When Samuel (Ethan Hawke) is torn from his daughter and sent to a brutal prison, Warden Clancy (Russell Crowe) offers him a high-stakes proposition: smuggle gold out of a remote mine with a dangerous crew of prisoners, and he'll win his freedom.

It's stripped-down as can be, but that doesn't stop it from being incredibly tense, with a particularly memorable scene unfolding on a sketchy drawbridge in what appears to be a direct nod to Sorcerer, albeit under very different circumstances. The Weight manages to convey its huge stakes despite its humble budget.

What other critics are saying: Reviews are very strong. The AP's Lindsay Bahr writes, "It is very much a 'dad movie,' which isn't, in this case, a bad or even limiting thing. More than a few people have compared it to something Clint Eastwood might have done at some point — just a solid, hearty, meat-and-potatoes kind of movie." David Fear at Rolling Stone says it's "not a perfect homage to 1970s tough-guy action flicks. But The Weight is close enough to give you that same thrill you get when, say, an old-timey James Coburn or Lee Marvin movie unexpectedly shows up on TCM."

How to watch: The Weight is now playing in select theaters.

Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom : The third feature-length film in this stop-motion animated series from Aardman Animations (the team behind Wallace & Gromit ) is a brisk Halloween-season delight that's highly recommended for all ages. On Halloween Eve at Mossy Bottom Farm, excitement turns to dismay when the clumsy Farmer ruins the pumpkin patch. Shaun tries fixing it with science experiments, but things go wrong when a wild beast appears in the woods. It has so many jokes and gags that you'll laugh a ton, and also be impressed by how well it works without a single line of dialogue. It's essentially a silent film for children. There are subtle visual gags throughout too, so keep your eyes peeled. Get tickets

The History of Concrete : John Wilson of HBO's beloved docuseries How To with John Wilson makes his feature debut with this hilarious, idiosyncratic and totally on-brand documentary that's ostensibly about, well, the history of concrete. But in the process, it's really about the human experience. It's not as pretentious and lofty as that sounds — in fact, it's as laugh-out-loud hysterical as it is insightful and purely fascinating. Wilson's fans are in for a treat, as it plays pretty much identically to his series, though it does gesture a bit toward some deeper and perhaps darker revelations about society. (You may find yourself wondering, "What do Chef Boyardee, or a guy who hands out free booze at liquor stores, have to do with the idea here?") But in a uniquely John Wilsonian fashion, it all feels quite revelatory and makes perfect sense by the end. It works great as an introduction to his sensibilities as a documentarian for newcomers and functions just as well as an expansion of his television work for those familiar. Get tickets

The buzziest release: The End of Oak Street

Why I liked it: J.J. Abrams already made his own feature-length approximation of a Steven Spielberg flick with Super 8 back in 2011, and now he's here producing another one 15 years later. Never change, J.J.!

David Robert Mitchell's The End of Oak Street plays like the most exciting Jurassic Park sequel never made: an old-fashioned Amblin-style, otherworldly adventure about a deteriorating family unit in the suburbs that reveals the cracks in the idyllic white-picket-fence American dream.

After a mysterious cosmic event rips Oak Street from suburbia and transports their neighborhood to an unknown place, the Platt family (headed by Anne Hathaway, continuing her very busy year, and Ewan McGregor) soon discovers that their very survival depends on sticking together as they navigate their now-unrecognizable surroundings.

On a formal level, the craft is often astonishing, decidedly showy yet still impressive, full of so many split-diopter shots that there's at one point a split-diopter shot reverse split-diopter shot. Mitchell, writer/director of the breakout horror hit It Follows, expertly mines the situation for maximum tension; the movie is essentially one dinosaur chase set piece after another. Sometimes it's a big one; other times it's the longest and biggest snake you've ever seen quietly slithering through a house, unbeknownst to its occupants. There's a lot of "dinosaurs lurking in the background that nobody notices," and it's effective damn near every time.

It's a satisfying blockbuster that just wants to entertain and deliver crowd-pleasing summer entertainment. There are, absolutely, bigger ideas at play here — a suburban street literally transported back in time carries a lot of thematic weight — but the movie isn't full of hokey messaging, despite arguably being "about" something. Is it a movie about the dangers of a society that's afraid to move forward and would rather go back to the way things once were? Maybe, but it's mostly just a vehicle for dinosaurs to violently kill a bunch of people in a highly populated, non-prehistoric setting. It's as if that one sequence from The Lost World were the whole movie, or like a Twilight Zone episode with a dino-sized budget. It's got a strange, uncanny quality to it that I associate with M. Night Shyamalan too.

The End of Oak Street may make some questionable narrative decisions in the final act, but none of that detracts from it being a terrifically good time at the movies. Mitchell's film ends up playing like a better 2026 Spielberg movie than the actual one . Ouch!

What other critics are saying : Reviews are leaning positive. Robbie Collin at the Telegraph writes that the film "isn't merely a running buffet of references; it's an honorable attempt to revive bygone blockbusting techniques for a contemporary crowd." But Kristy Puchko at Mashable wasn't into it, writing, "If you're looking for carefree summer fun, look elsewhere. The End of Oak Street is not fun. It's bleak, brutal and ultimately infuriating."

How to watch : The End of Oak Street is now available to rent or buy on Apple TV , Prime Video and other VOD platforms.

Why I liked it: Canadian filmmaker Matt Johnson ( Nirvanna the Band the Show the Movie , BlackBerry) leaps into the mainstream with Tony, a melancholy yet always charming coming-of-age dramedy. It also happens to be a biopic about Anthony Bourdain, covering a very specific chapter of the late chef's early days, loosely adapted from his breakthrough book, Kitchen Confidential .

A 19-year-old Bourdain travels to Provincetown and stumbles into the chaotic world of a restaurant kitchen, setting off a summer that will shape the course of his life. The movie opens with a quote from the book: "I was — to be frank — a spoiled, miserable, narcissistic, self-destructive and thoughtless young lout, and badly in need of a good ass-kicking." In this movie, he gets that ass-kicking. But does it help?

Dominic Sessa, the breakout star of The Holdovers, is transcendent here, perfectly embodying Bourdain and the specific way he speaks, without ever feeling like he's doing a cheap imitation or impression. It's such a brooding portrayal and appropriately gloomy without ever crossing into discomfort, given that the audience is likely aware of how Bourdain's story ends.

Antonio Banderas nearly steals the show as the restaurant owner who takes young Bourdain in at his lowest point and helps him become the man we know he would become. Leo Woodall is another standout in the exact opposite role, the proverbial devil on his shoulder, a ladies' man with a drug addiction whose presence in the movie clearly means to show us another path Bourdain could've easily taken. Comedian Stavros Halkias, meanwhile, earns lots of laughs as a foul-mouthed line cook.

It's beautifully shot by Michael Bauman, the Oscar-nominated cinematographer of One Battle After Another , and the gorgeous '70s Cape Cod summer sights really pop, helping evoke an extremely cozy, low-stakes hangout vibe. The dreamy, delicate and sad score from frequent Johnson collaborator Jay McCarrol enhances that atmosphere perfectly.

The film manages to avoid lots of biopic clichés and pitfalls, though it also engages in a couple, including a fairly thankless role for Emilia Jones as Bourdain's love interest. (She is nevertheless very good.) It's a coming-of-age story that feels honest and true, deeply felt in its depiction of its lead as an unapologetic a**hole, but a well-meaning one who is young and just trying to find himself.

Tony is impressive on both a craft and story level, all the better for being content to be more of a hangout movie with an unbeatable vibe than a traditional life-to-death biopic. There's just a warmth to everything here, from the texture of the photography to its characters.

What other critics are saying: It's getting great reviews. Amy Nicholson at the Los Angeles Times writes, "The kitchen scenes are a combo platter of boot camp, frat house hazing ritual and kung fu movie. As Bourdain would later explain, he thrived in a setting where actions have instant consequences: a sore back, a sliced hand, a good meal." A.V. Club's Monica Castillo writes, "Beyond its dutiful biopic services, Tony reminds its audience of the sharp turns and unlikely encounters that can change the course of our lives and give us stories to share over the dinner table."

How to watch : Tony is now available to rent or buy on Apple TV , Prime Video and other VOD platforms.

Another option: The Rivals of Amziah King

Why I liked it: This genre-bending indie gem starring Matthew McConaughey (read our interview with him here ) is wholly unique, incredibly charming and has a few moments of genuine "movies don't get any better than this" transcendence. It's also incredibly hard to describe because of its singular nature, but I'll try my best. It plays like an adaptation of a great American novel that doesn't exist — and is easily the most I've ever been moved by a movie that features someone being unexpectedly and graphically scalped.

McConaughey plays the eponymous Amziah King, a beekeeper, musician and anchor of his community who reunites with former foster daughter Kateri (newcomer Angelina LookingGlass), after many years apart while fending off threats to his honey business.

The first hour of the movie contains pretty much all of the aforementioned transcendence, and while it struggles to follow up on that exciting, good-natured and infectious energy, it still manages to stick the landing. There are simple sequences here where Amziah and his buddies strike up a tune, and the power and importance of community shine through in a way that nearly moved me to tears. Amziah is the glue that holds this particular one together, and despite knowing nothing about him up top, you almost immediately get a sense of who he is as a person and local figurehead.

McConaughey is excellent — the best he's been in ages and maybe ever, channeling that relaxed, cool-guy persona that he so effortlessly does. LookingGlass is a breakout presence here, basically becoming the lead character as the movie stretches on. It's a hell of an introductory role.

The film plays a bit like a Western, then becomes a Southern-fried musical and a Coen Brothers-style crime flick before morphing into a moving drama about a father and a daughter, and, eventually, a revenge thriller. Somehow, it manages to feel lived-in and on course the entire time.

The Rivals of Amziah King is a joyful movie full of unexpected detours and digressions that ultimately feels like a celebration of connecting with those around you. There's not a cellphone in sight here, just people living in the moment. It's a message that feels increasingly important in our siloed, filter-bubbled times.

What other critics are saying: Most love it! Daily Beast's Nick Schager writes, "As subtly sharp as it is sweet, it's one of the year's most enlivening standouts." Mark Kennedy at the AP , however, dinged it for not feeling "authentic." I disagree!

How to watch : The Rivals of Amziah King is now available to rent or buy on Apple TV, Prime Video and other VOD platforms.

It Ends : I never connected with this surreal, minimalist, no-budget indie, an alleged thriller about a group of recent college graduates who get stuck on a road that simply won't end. The entire thing is meant to be taken as a metaphor for life itself — more specifically, about the existential dread people of that age might face nowadays amid the pandemic, AI and other developments that make the transition from childhood to adulthood fraught and the future uncertain. There may be enough meat on the bone for an episode of The Twilight Zone, but it bored me at feature length. Maybe if it engaged with the supernatural horrors on the periphery instead of going all in on its central metaphor, it would've been more fun. Your mileage may vary. Rent or buy

Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma : Jane Schoenbrun's follow-up to the extremely personal I Saw the TV Glow is arguably even more personal, exploring an extremely specific feeling while saying so much about horror movies, sexuality, identity, shame, and the intersection of all these things that it doesn't matter if you don't personally connect to every single element. Unlike its predecessor, which is deeply moving but also fairly humorless, Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma is laugh-out-loud funny and joyful. It couldn't be further in tone from TV Glow despite exploring similar ideas. It's fun ! Read my full review here . Rent or buy.

Nimrods : Fans of the band Green Day may enjoy this Green Day-produced movie about Green Day that features Green Day, but it's not really for anybody else. Three friends journey from Kansas City to Los Angeles, mistakenly believing their band is opening for Green Day on New Year's Eve after a prank pulled by one of their brothers. The ingredients for a fun, raunchy road trip comedy are here, but it just isn't very funny or charming, and my interest in the band had long waned by the time I graduated high school. Again, their loyal fans will likely get a kick out of it. Rent or buy

📺 Movies newly available on streaming services you may already have

Why I liked it: I'd never heard of this movie or anybody in it, but that didn't matter in the slightest. I was quickly charmed by its two stars and the familiar but functional coming-of-age story told through a very culturally specific lens that you don't often see in teen and college movies like this.

Maitreyi Ramakrishnan and Priyanka Kedia star as childhood best friends, Maya and Anjali, who join their college's competitive Bollywood dance team only to discover that the road to winning the national championship is far more raucous and cutthroat than they ever imagined.

The plot itself is totally formulaic, but the characters are both so lived-in and real-feeling that it's easy to be charmed by them and care for their personal journeys. The specifics of the world here are unique and exciting; simply put, the impressive choreography, theatrics and spectacle of Bollywood dance are a lot of fun to watch, and the movie does a good job of presenting them.

Best of the Best plays as if the teen classic Bring It On or something like Step Up were about competitive Bollywood dancing instead of cheerleading and hip-hop dancing, respectively. If that sounds good to you, you will enjoy it, and it's got heart and laughs to boot. It's a real crowd-pleaser!

What other critics are saying : They agree with my take! William Bibbiani at TheWrap says, "The entire ensemble is fantastic, even if most of the actors are playing whimsical archetypes." IndieWire's Allison Foreman writes, "Even when it wraps things up a little too conveniently, Best of the Best leaves you wanting a movie more like a traditional three-hour Bollywood affair."

How to watch : Best of the Best is now streaming on Netflix .

Why I didn't like it: Horror movies are often predicated upon people making stupid decisions, and Goody Goody really pushes the limits of how much of that an audience can take.

It's a movie about a home birth gone horribly wrong, set in a remote cabin far from any hospitals during a blizzard — not an ideal combination for such an activity. The characters are the pregnant woman and her husband, his sister, a doula, and their midwife, who initially tries to keep the expectant mother calm and in the dark as the problems begin. Eventually, the husband disappears, and then the s*** really hits the fan.

There have been so many movies — especially as of late — about the horrors of pregnancy and childbirth and the general terrors of motherhood, including another recent Shudder movie called Nightborn , that it's now its own subgenre.

Despite bringing some potent ideas to the table, Goody Goody doesn't do much with them. Midwives and caretakers gaslighting someone into thinking everything is OK during a dangerous birth is a terrifying idea, and I wish the movie had stayed grounded in the more realistic human tragedy of it all, rather than the cosmic and/or supernatural places it goes. It's a badly paced bore in which you're waiting for characters to catch up with what the audience already knows.

Goody Goody does feature what has to be the nastiest and most upsetting birth sequence I've ever seen, which might be enough for the gorehounds, but the road there just isn't very compelling.

What other critics are saying : There aren't many reviews posted yet, but the field is split thus far. The Guardian's Phil Hoad writes, "Amid the mayhem, [director Raymond] Creamer still manages the odd visual flourish. … But if Goody Goody really had to take The Omen route, he needed to deliver the transition with far more delicacy." Cheryl Eddy at io9 was into it, writing, "The magic here comes more from Creamer's direction — lots of close-ups, careful framing and creative lighting — and his cast and crew."

How to watch : Goody Goody is now streaming on Shudder.

That's all for this week! We'll see you next Friday.

articles.title: ‘VIBE’ X (Twitter) review: Kunal Kemmu and Preity Zinta’s comedy gets warm audience response, fans call it ‘best comedy film of this year’ as audiences praise its humour
articles.summary: Kunal Kemmu and Preity Zinta’s new film ‘VIBE’ has received a largely warm response from audiences on X (formerly Twitter), with several early viewers.
articles.body: Kunal Kemmu and Preity Zinta’s new film ‘VIBE’ has received a largely warm response from audiences on X (formerly Twitter), with several early viewers praising its humour, ensemble cast and Kemmu’s work as both actor and director. Some viewers have even described the film as one of the standout comedies of the year so far.While much of the early reaction has been positive, a few viewers raised concerns about the second half, screenplay, action sequences and music, offering a more mixed assessment of the film as a whole.Theatre or OTT? Viewers weigh in on ‘VIBE’A key point of discussion among early viewers has been whether ‘VIBE’ works best as a theatrical experience or would have been better suited to streaming. Several users have encouraged audiences to watch the film in theatres, specifically praising the performances of Kunal Kemmu, Preity Zinta, Sparsh Srivastava and Vanshika Dhir.One viewer revealed that they watched ‘VIBE’ in a nearly empty theatre with only seven other people but still came away impressed by the film. According to the post, the story begins in Mumbai before moving to Bangkok for its climax. The viewer also clarified that ‘VIBE’ has no connection with ‘Madgaon Express’.The post praised the ensemble cast and described Kunal Kemmu’s writing, direction and performance as “top notch”. Sparsh Srivastava was singled out for his performance, with the viewer saying he “absolutely killed it” and highlighting his versatility across projects of different scales.The same viewer felt that Dinesh Lal Yadav’s character did not work as well, while praising Yashpal Sharma’s performance. Vanshika Dhir’s character and accent also received appreciation. However, the viewer felt Preity Zinta was not the ideal fit for her role and suggested that another actor might have suited the part better.Despite those reservations, the viewer strongly recommended experiencing ‘VIBE’ in theatres, praising its writing and describing it as a film worth supporting.‘VIBE’ called ‘the best comedy film of this year till date’ by viewerAnother X user offered an emphatic response, describing ‘VIBE’ as “the best comedy film of this year till date”. The viewer also praised Kunal Kemmu’s performance and his work behind the camera, calling him “insane” in his dual role as actor and filmmaker.A third viewer described ‘VIBE’ as the most entertaining film they had watched recently, particularly highlighting the audience reaction inside the theatre. They said the entire auditorium was laughing throughout the screening, something they claimed was a rare experience.The viewer praised the film as clean, balanced and heavily focused on comedy, while also highlighting performances by Preity Zinta and Kunal Kemmu. They concluded by expressing their support for what they described as “organic comedy”.While the early X reactions are largely positive, audience responses remain mixed on certain aspects of the film, particularly its second half and some technical elements. The social-media conversation, however, indicates that the comedy and performances are among the aspects generating the most discussion.More about ‘VIBE’Directed by Kunal Kemmu, ‘VIBE’ stars Kunal Kemmu, Preity Zinta, Sparsh Shrivastava, Yashpal Sharma and Vanshika Dhir.The film was released in theatres on September 18, 2026.Get the latest Bollywood & Entertainment News, and more. articles.title: Kings of Leon presentan su 10º álbum de estudio, 'O My Beloved'
articles.standfirst: La banda recupera el espíritu crudo y directo de la música que hacían cuando llegaron por primera vez a Nashville
articles.summary: La banda recupera el espíritu crudo y directo de la música que hacían cuando llegaron por primera vez a Nashville
articles.body: kings of Leon anunció su décimo álbum de estudio de larga duración, 'O My Beloved', que se publicará el 6 de noviembre a través de Love Tap Records / Virgin Music Group Con 'O My Beloved', Kings of Leon presentan un trabajo sin filtros, el más íntimo hasta la fecha. Una colección de canciones que reflexiona sobre el devenir de la banda, sus experiencias y el camino que los ha llevado hasta donde están hoy. Es su primer álbum de larga duración producido íntegramente por ellos mismos, y da vida por completo a su visión creativa colectiva, dando como resultado un sonido profundamente personal e inequívocamente suyo. Alejado del sonido expansivo que ha definido buena parte de su carrera, el álbum recupera el espíritu crudo y directo de la música que hacían cuando llegaron por primera vez a Nashville. Profundamente personales y centradas en la gratitud, la familia y el aprecio por la vida que han construido juntos, las canciones retratan a los hombres y padres en los que se han convertido, encontrando significado en las personas, los recuerdos y los momentos cotidianos que han dado forma a sus vidas. Como una carta de amor a su familia y al camino que los ha traído hasta aquí, 'O My Beloved' ofrece una mirada íntima a los cuatro miembros y al viaje que han compartido. “Ya hemos superado todo lo que alguna vez imaginamos que podríamos conseguir y hemos construido algo muy especial. Pensé: ¿no sería precioso hacer un álbum que mirara hacia atrás, a todo lo que hemos hecho, y apreciara cómo hemos llegado hasta aquí?”, afirma el vocalista Caleb Followill. “En las canciones aparecen nuestras familias, historias de nuestra infancia, cosas que quizá en su momento no parecían tan importantes, pero la forma en que acaban encontrando su lugar en estas canciones me hace darme cuenta de lo mucho que realmente influyeron en mi vida.” Coincidiendo con el anuncio del álbum, Kings of Leon han publicado 'My Whole World', el primer single de 'O My Beloved'. La canción nació de un lugar profundamente personal, dejando que recuerdos y emociones conservados durante años encontraran su camino hacia la música. El resultado es una introducción cargada de emoción al álbum y un anticipo del lado más vulnerable de Kings of Leon que recorre todo el disco.

articles.title: Reaction to ‘Ted Lasso’ shows left-wing critics are never satisfied, so why does Hollywood keep trying?
articles.summary: 'Ted Lasso' Season 4 built its entire plot around women's soccer and feminist themes, yet progressive critics still said the show failed women.
articles.body: Apple’s major hit show "Ted Lasso" centered its return on women’s soccer and nearly every grievance progressive critics prioritize. They still said it failed women. It should serve as a reminder to Hollywood that trying to please people who are never satisfied is a losing battle. And Hollywood really should stop ruining good shows trying to chase that approval. Now, I loved the first two seasons of "Ted Lasso." The third season wasn't as good, but I watched the entire thing. So, when Apple brought the show back after a three-year hiatus, I was willing to give Season 4 a chance. I didn't make it through the premiere. During the opening sequence, Ted is working at a Kansas City grocery store and casually stealing food from his employer. When a coworker asks whether he worries about getting caught, Ted says he doesn't, "probably due to my deeply ingrained white male privilege." It was a throwaway joke that arrived almost immediately, before the show established its new story or gave viewers much of a reason to care. It felt deliberate, like the writers were telling the audience exactly what kind of season this would be. RIDICULOUS USA TODAY COLUMN PROVES THAT THE DEMAND FOR MISOGYNY IN SPORTS FAR EXCEEDS THE SUPPLY Then came the Negro Leagues Baseball Museum scene. Leslie Higgins visits the museum after discovering that the American Jazz Museum is closed for a private event. A tour guide explains how Black baseball players, including Satchel Paige, were denied opportunities in Major League Baseball because of segregation. Higgins responds by comparing their experience to women once being prohibited from playing soccer in England. Using the color barrier in American baseball as a narrative bridge to the challenges facing a fictional English women's soccer team felt painfully forced and over-the-top. My wife rolled her eyes. I looked at her and asked whether there was any reason to keep watching. She agreed there wasn't. So, we turned it off. I couldn't stomach watching the remaining episodes, but I did review the transcripts of all seven that Apple has released as of Sept. 17. I paid particularly close attention to the first four episodes, which were among those provided to television critics before the season premiered. Those transcripts confirmed exactly what the opening episode suggested: Gender politics aren't a minor component of the new season. They are the season. ‘Ted Lasso’ made its priorities clear from the beginning The second episode revolves heavily around whether Rebecca is sufficiently feminist after hiring Ted to coach AFC Richmond's new women's team. Alice Chilton, who helped construct the team, tells Rebecca she is resigning after being passed over for the head-coaching position. Before leaving, Alice asks Rebecca whether she considered her for the job. Rebecca says no. Alice then asks whether Rebecca considered any woman. Again, Rebecca says no. This sends Rebecca into a panic over whether she is supportive enough of women. She begins reading feminist literature and delivers a painfully awkward press-conference speech declaring that women are "just as capable and compelling as men" and that "the future is female." She then introduces the manager of Richmond's women's team, "who just happens to be a man." The show plays Rebecca's desperation for laughs. But the underlying conflict is whether Ted, as a man, should have received the opportunity at all. Remember what Ted accomplished with Richmond. He took the club through relegation, earned promotion back to the Premier League and then led it to second place after entering the final day of the season with a chance to win the championship. Ted was overqualified to coach a brand-new second-division women's team. Yet the show treats Rebecca's decision to hire him as evidence that she might have failed women. The first four episodes introduce several predictable progressive talking points surrounding supposed oppression of women in sports: lower salaries, inferior facilities, inadequate media coverage and a lack of financial support. One might argue that those are products of capitalism and not some nefarious plot to hold down female athletes, but I digress. Then comes a cascade of storylines centered on female athletes, as if the writers had a checklist and had to make sure they hit them all. One player leaves the team after becoming pregnant. A single mother brings her child to open tryouts because she couldn't arrange childcare. Sponsors threaten to abandon the team, while male shareholders mock the entire idea as a waste of money. Then Zelda Southport, a wealthy investor in women's sports, delivers a speech accusing executives of using women's soccer for "reputation-laundering" while hiding their "fake allyship." She invokes the "patriarchy" for good measure. Again, the writers aren't trying to hide their political messaging. Quite the opposite, in fact. The political messaging is the entire plot. The promotional campaign made the target audience equally clear On Aug. 5, the day Season 4 premiered, "Ted Lasso" co-creator Brendan Hunt appeared on Sarah Spain's podcast. Spain is a radical left-wing activist who has referred to Vice President J.D. Vance as a "demon" and launched a disgusting personal smear of Sophie Cunningham for having the temerity to argue against "biological men" in women's sports. Hunt chose Spain's show to help promote the new season, which felt like a very intentional promotional choice. The following night, Jason Sudeikis, Hunt, Juno Temple and several members of the new cast appeared at an exclusive "Ted Lasso" event at the Paley Museum. Megan Rapinoe, another radical far-left-wing activist, served as the moderator. The people behind "Ted Lasso" knew whose approval they wanted and went directly to Sarah Spain and Megan Rapinoe to seek it. The interview with Hunt also made clear how central the women's team was to the show's return. He said Sudeikis kept thinking about doing the series with a women's team after Season 3. That idea led to a small writers' retreat intended to determine whether the show remained "fertile ground." The writers decided it did. In other words, women's soccer wasn't simply the setting selected after the decision to revive "Ted Lasso." It was the idea that convinced the creators to revive it. Apple celebrated the premiere, but what happened afterward? Despite my reaction, plenty of people watched the Season 4 premiere. According to Nielsen data provided by Apple, the episode generated 296.6 million viewing minutes in the United States across Aug. 4 and Aug. 5. More than 200 million minutes came on Aug. 5 alone, making "Ted Lasso" the most-streamed program in the country that day. Apple called it the biggest launch in Apple TV history. That's impressive, but it also isn't terribly surprising. "Ted Lasso" was one of the most popular streaming shows in America during its original run. It won 13 Emmy Awards, became Apple's signature television series and disappeared for three years after what many viewers believed was its finale. Of course people wanted to see it return. Nielsen's first weekly report was also strong. "Ted Lasso" generated 866 million viewing minutes across 35 available episodes, including the first three seasons, during the week of Aug. 3 through Aug. 9. The Season 4 premiere accounted for 36% of that total, and the show ranked second among streaming originals. But those figures establish only that people were interested in the return of "Ted Lasso." They don't tell us whether the audience stuck around as the season progressed. OutKick/Fox News Digital reached out to Apple and asked for episode-by-episode viewing totals for the subsequent Season 4 episodes. We also asked whether the company had internal data showing how many viewers who started the premiere finished it and continued watching the season. Apple did not respond. The company eagerly supplied the figure that allowed it to announce the biggest premiere in the history of its streaming service. It became much less communicative when asked for the numbers that would show whether those viewers kept watching. If the later episodes were setting similarly historic marks, it is reasonable to think Apple would be just as eager to publicize those numbers. Instead, the company that celebrated the premiere hasn't released any viewing data on the show in over a month. While that doesn't prove viewership collapsed after the premiere, there is no public evidence that the record-setting launch translated into equally historic retention. Progressive critics still thought the show failed women TIME critic Judy Berman received the first four episodes of Season 4 for review. So, she saw Ted invoke his "white male privilege," Rebecca admit that she never considered a woman for the coaching job, Alice confront her over that decision, players struggle with pregnancy and childcare, sponsors abandon the women's team and wealthy investors get lectured about the patriarchy and their "fake allyship." The show couldn't have worked harder to establish its progressive credentials. Despite all of that, Berman's headline read: "Ted Lasso Doesn't Know What to Do With Women's Soccer." Berman argued that Ted's presence could come across as "paternalistic" and said the character sometimes resembled a "cringey, try-hard male feminist." She complained that Rebecca and Keeley still felt filtered through the "male gaze" and noted that many qualified female coaches could have received Ted's job. "A different coach is going to have to inspire those locker rooms, because Ted Lasso just doesn't belong," she concluded. You know, for a group of people who constantly complain that men think women "don't belong" in sports, they sure don't seem to have a problem proclaiming that men don't belong in women's sports. Well, except the men who "identify" as women, of course. Those men are to be celebrated. The Times of London critic Carol Midgley criticized the decision to sideline Alice in favor of Ted and argued that other storylines played into gender stereotypes, concluding that "occasionally you could argue the show itself is sexist." Apparently, building the season around women's sports, sexism, representation, unequal funding and male privilege wasn't enough. Even one of the people enlisted to celebrate the season found another way the show elevated a man at women's expense. At the end of Spain's interview with Hunt, she recounted a conversation in which Malala Yousafzai argued that the series should really be called "Rebecca." Her reasoning was that Ted's compassionate coaching style is possible only because Rebecca, as the club's owner, permits it. Spain said Malala believed a male owner would have fired Ted and hired a more traditionally masculine manager. Spain later asked Sudeikis what he thought of Malala's argument. "They're not changing the name," he replied, according to Spain. Hunt was far more accommodating. Spain quoted him calling Malala "incredible" and saying, "Everything she says makes sense," before joking that Warner Bros. probably didn't want to relabel all the merchandise. Think about the moving target here. "Ted Lasso" resurrected itself around a women's team, filled its opening episodes with feminist grievances, pushed its title character toward the sidelines and promoted the season alongside Sarah Spain and Megan Rapinoe. The response was still that the woman wasn't receiving enough credit and perhaps the man's name should be removed from the title. As of this writing, Season 4 holds an 88% critics score and a 69% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes. Based on those numbers, critics generally approved of the season's direction more than the audience did, yet prominent progressive reviewers still found new ideological shortcomings to condemn. What was "Ted Lasso" supposed to do? Hollywood keeps chasing approval it can never earn Hollywood studios repeatedly bend popular franchises around the demands of progressive critics. Writers center the "correct" political issues, diversify the cast, elevate female characters and turn familiar stories into vehicles for approved social messages. The audience gets a less entertaining product and critics still aren't satisfied. So, what's the point? You see, for the left-wing media, satisfaction would undermine the entire industry. A critic whose influence comes from identifying perceived sexism, racism, homophobia, transphobia and whatever other "isms" and "phobias" they will invent in the next few years has little incentive to declare that a mainstream television show handled everything correctly. The standard changes because the criticism is the product. Hollywood keeps playing along, presumably because executives want favorable coverage, awards and protection from the online backlash that comes with refusing to follow the approved script. SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER The show's creators resurrected a beloved series and rebuilt it around the issues progressive television critics claim to care about most. They then took it directly to sympathetic figures in left-wing sports media for promotion. The progressive critics still weren't happy. At some point, Hollywood might consider making shows for the people watching them instead of people professionally committed to manufacturing grievances on behalf of whichever "marginalized group" the show has supposedly wronged.

articles.title: Katrina Kaif faces trolling over post-pregnancy body, Hrithik Roshan shows support as he likes post calling out trolls: ‘Your commentary on her won’t affect her'
articles.summary: Katrina Kaif’s appearance at the Ambani family’s Ganesh Chaturthi celebrations in Mumbai on September 14 sparked an unexpected conversation online. Th.
articles.body: Katrina Kaif’s appearance at the Ambani family’s Ganesh Chaturthi celebrations in Mumbai on September 14 sparked an unexpected conversation online. The actor, who attended the festivities with husband Vicky Kaushal, found herself at the centre of social media commentary about her post-pregnancy body, with some users making comparisons to her older photographs. The criticism did not go unnoticed, as several fans called out the body-shaming, while a post defending Katrina also received a like from Hrithik Roshan.Amid the debate, an Instagram post by Harshveer Jain, who goes by the handle storysellercomics, gained attention. The creator shared a two-slide post addressing the comments surrounding Katrina’s appearance and also opened up about his own admiration for the actor.In the first slide, Harshveer recalled being a Katrina fan during his teenage years. He wrote, “I crushed on Katrina Kaif all my teenage. Travelled inter-state to catch a glimpse. Kept newspaper cutouts and movie posters, some even in my wallet. Watched movies because she was casted. And now when a troll says she’s finished because she put on post-pregnancy weight, I can only pity that troll.”The second slide addressed teenagers who may not understand why comments about Katrina’s body are being labelled as trolling. It read, “So if you are a teenager who is confused as to why are people calling you a troll for commenting on Katrina Kaif’s apparent weight gain, please note that —She is a mother. She has a successful business. Signs of a fairly successful life, personal and professional. Your commentary on her won’t affect her. You are a nobody for her. But women around you will look at that and immediately both, be hurt and also take you for a woman hater. Hopefully, you don’t want either.”Hrithik Roshan, who has shared screen space with Katrina in ‘Bang Bang’ and ‘Zindagi Na Milegi Dobara’, also appeared to endorse the sentiment by liking the post. The actor did not leave a comment or make a separate statement about the trolling.Meanwhile, Katrina’s recent pictures and videos have prompted some social media users to compare her present appearance with her earlier looks. Some comments went beyond discussing her appearance, with users claiming that the actor was “finished” because of the changes to her body after pregnancy. One X user wrote, “I wonder what happened to the Katrina we used to see” . Another commented on her age, saying she “looks older than Rekha ji”.However, many fans pushed back against the criticism and pointed out that Katrina became a mother less than a year ago. The actor welcomed her son Vihaan in November 2025. One user wrote, “She’s 43. She had a baby. Her body changed. That’s literally how biology works” .Others argued that reducing Katrina’s journey to her appearance overlooked her career, business and personal life. One social media user wrote, “Has a successful 400-crore business, a wonderful partner, a beautiful baby and an iconic film career. Do you have even half of that?” .Katrina is also not the only Bollywood actor to have faced scrutiny over her body after embracing motherhood. Aishwarya Rai Bachchan faced intense commentary about her appearance following the birth of her daughter Aaradhya in 2011 and continues to face social media trolling over her looks. Richa Chadha, Swara Bhasker and Bipasha Basu have also spoken about the expectations and pressure women in the public eye face regarding their bodies after pregnancy.Katrina, meanwhile, has largely stayed away from the spotlight in recent months as she focuses on motherhood and her business ventures. articles.title: Duncan Sheik, ‘Barely Breathing’ singer, dead at 56
articles.summary: Duncan Sheik, the voice behind "Barely Breathing" and Tony-winning "Spring Awakening," died from organ failure at 56, his mother confirmed.
articles.body: Duncan Sheik, the singer-songwriter behind the hit "Barely Breathing" and the Tony and Grammy-winning musical "Spring Awakening," has died. He was 56. Sheik died Thursday from organ failure, his mother, Suzanne Sheik, told The New York Times. Representatives for Sheik did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment. HOLLYWOOD STARS WHO DIED IN 2026: PHOTOS "It is with profound sadness that we confirm the passing of Duncan Sheik. The world has a lost a singular talent, and deeply influential voice in music and theater," Sheik’s social media account posted Friday. "Duncan was a father, husband, son, brother, and friend. He will be remembered for his sensitivity, wit, intelligence, and depth of spirit he brought to those who knew and loved him." The news comes after Sheik’s Instagram account shared an update on his health on Wednesday. "Duncan is currently receiving medical care and remains in critical but stable condition," the statement read. "Out of respect for Duncan and our family, we will not be sharing any further medical details at this time." "We kindly ask for privacy during this incredibly difficult time and will provide updates when appropriate," the statement continued. "Thank you for the continued love and support." Throughout the summer of 2026, Sheik frequently posted photos of himself from the hospital on Instagram. He did not publicly share details about his condition. His song "Barely Breathing," released in 1996, spent 55 weeks on the Billboard Hot 100, peaking at No. 16. The song earned Sheik a Grammy nomination for best male pop vocal performance in 1998 and later found new audiences on shows including "Glee" and "Girls." His other projects included "Whisper House," "Legerdemain" and the 2022 album "Claptrap." articles.title: Formula One driver Lewis Hamilton tells Macklemore he is ‘standing’ in solidarity with him on Palestine
articles.summary: Lewis Hamilton pledged to stand in solidarity with Macklemore after his "Free Palestine" messaging got him removed from Ed Sheeran's "Loop Tour."
articles.body: Pop star Macklemore has generated quite a buzz recently with his "Free Palestine" messaging while on Ed Sheeran's "Loop Tour." The 43-year-old musician was kicked off the tour following backlash from his pro-Palestine stance, but there have been a few "woke" celebrities who have come to Macklemore's defense. Following the Seattle native's pledge to donate $1 million to Palestinian aid organizations, children's YouTube star Ms. Rachel said she would match his donation and urged "every wealthy White celebrity" to do the same. MACKLEMORE DONATES $1M TO PALESTINIAN AID ORGANIZATIONS AFTER ED SHEERAN TOUR FALLOUT Ms. Rachel isn't the only one to throw her public support behind Macklemore, though, as Formula One driver Lewis Hamilton took to social media to praise the rapper for his stance. Hamilton commented under Macklemore's Instagram statement on the matter, pledging to "stand" in solidarity with him. COLIN KAEPERNICK ACCUSES NFL OF 'COLLUDING' AGAINST MACKLEMORE AMID 'FREE PALESTINE' CONTROVERSY If you know anything about Hamilton, then this shouldn't come as a shock. The 41-year-old was at the forefront of the Black Lives Matter movement, especially when it reached a fever pitch following the death of George Floyd in 2020. Hamilton took part in the protesting of the U.S. National Anthem, kneeling during its playing before every Grand Prix event he entered in that same year. He's been spotted wearing shirts supporting causes linked to Black Lives Matter quite often and has also been a vocal supporter of LGBTQ+ issues. Between those incidents and his past comments about Formula One's lack of diversity - Hamilton is mixed-race and is the only Black driver in the sport - it's easy to see why he was so quick to jump on the bandwagon to support Macklemore for his pro-Palestine stance. As others continue to excoriate the rapper for his "Free Palestine" messaging, such as Barstool founder Dave Portnoy, you can expect many more on the other side of the aisle to voice their support for him.
